 Best RV Power Station 2026: Boondocking & Shore-Power Backup Picks
 By Editorial Team · Updated October 6, 2026
 Affiliate disclosure: We independently research and test every product. When you buy through links on this page, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Quick answer
 The EcoFlow Delta 2 Max is the best RV power station for most rigs: 2,048Wh of LiFePO4 capacity,
2,400W continuous output (3,400W with X-Boost), and a compact footprint that fits in a cabinet or
storage bay. It recharges from solar, shore power, or your tow vehicle’s 12V outlet, which matters more
in an RV than in a tent. Boondockers who need to run heavier loads or want true whole-rig backup should
size up to the EcoFlow Delta Pro , which pairs with a soft-start device to run a rooftop AC unit —
something no mid-size power station can do on its own.
 RV power needs sit in an odd middle ground: too big for a compact camping power station, too
demanding for a plug-and-charge phone battery, but usually smaller than a full home-backup system.
The units below are sized and specced for that gap — shore-power backup, boondocking runtime, and
appliances that draw more than a laptop or a string of lights.
 Why RV power is a different sizing problem
 According to RV Industry Association survey data, roughly 11 million U.S. households now own an RV,
and a growing share of that group boondocks off-grid rather than staying exclusively at powered
campsites — which is exactly the scenario where a power station replaces a noisy gas generator. The
catch is appliance load: a typical 13,500 BTU RV rooftop air conditioner needs a starting surge of
roughly 2,800-3,500 watts , per HVAC manufacturer specs, well beyond what a compact or mid-size power
station can deliver. Micro-Air, maker of the EasyStart soft-start module, states its device cuts that
starting surge by up to 70% , which is the reason soft-start add-ons show up so often in RV power
station discussions — without one, only the largest expandable units stand a chance at running
rooftop AC at all.

 1. EcoFlow Delta 2 Max — Best Overall
 EcoFlow Delta 2 Max (2,048Wh)
 Best overall for RVs · ~$799-1,299 · 2,048Wh LiFePO4 · 2,400W AC
 Compact enough for a cabinet, basement bay, or under-dinette storage — a real consideration in an RV where space is at a premium.
 Recharges from shore power, solar panels, or a car outlet, so it tops back up whether you're plugged in, boondocking, or driving between sites.
 Expandable to 6,144Wh with an add-on battery if a weekend rig turns into a longer trip.
 The Delta 2 Max earns the overall pick because it fits the shape of actual RV life: enough capacity
for a weekend of lights, fridge, water pump, and device charging, small enough to stow out of the way,
and flexible about how it recharges. It won’t run a rooftop AC, but for the appliances most RVers
actually run off-grid, it’s the best balance of capacity and footprint in this list. See our full
EcoFlow Delta 2 Max review for recharge-speed numbers and how
it compares to the step-up Delta Pro.
 2. EcoFlow Delta Pro — Best for Full-Time RVers & Rooftop AC
 EcoFlow Delta Pro (3,600Wh)
 Best for full-time / rooftop AC · ~$2,199-3,699 · 3,600Wh LiFePO4 · 3,600W AC
 3,600W continuous output (7,200W with X-Boost) is the closest a portable unit gets to running a rooftop AC — paired with a soft-start device, it's one of the few that can.
 Stacks to 25kWh with add-on batteries, which is what full-time and long-boondock RVers actually need for multi-day runtime.
 Works with EcoFlow's smart panel and solar input for a semi-permanent, generator-free RV power setup.
 If you live in your rig full-time or spend weeks off-grid, the Delta Pro is the unit that can actually
replace a generator rather than just supplement one. It costs more and takes up more storage, but it’s
the only power station on this list with a realistic shot at running a rooftop AC alongside everything
else. Rigs with a hardwired 240V load should also look at the
 Anker SOLIX F3800 , which pushes 6,000W continuous — well past
what any unit here can match.
 3. Anker SOLIX F2000 — Best Expandable
 Anker SOLIX F2000 (2,048Wh)
 Best expandable · ~$799-899 · 2,048Wh LiFePO4 · 2,400W AC
 Expandable to 6,144Wh with two add-on batteries, letting a weekend-trip setup grow into a longer-trip one without replacing the base unit.
 Rated for roughly 3,000 cycles to 80% capacity, useful given how often an RV power station gets cycled on a long road trip.
 2,400W continuous, 3,600W surge via SurgePad — covers a fridge, water pump, and electronics with headroom for a microwave.
 The F2000 is the pick for RVers who aren’t sure yet how much capacity they’ll ultimately want. Buying
the base unit now and adding batteries later is cheaper than guessing high on day one and it carries
Anker’s longer warranty coverage into the bargain. Read our full Anker SOLIX F2000
review for the complete breakdown.
 4. Bluetti AC180 — Best Compact & Budget
 Bluetti AC180 (1,152Wh)
 Best compact/budget · ~$499 · 1,152Wh LiFePO4 · 1,800W AC
 Smaller footprint suits a travel trailer or smaller Class B/C rig where storage space is tighter than a full-size Class A.
 1,800W continuous output covers lights, a fridge, water pump, and charging without the price of a 2kWh-class unit.
 Recharges quickly from solar (up to 500W input) for shorter boondocking stints between hookups.
 Not every rig needs a 2kWh-plus unit. For smaller trailers, truck campers, or RVers who mostly stay at
powered sites and just want backup for outages or short boondock stops, the AC180 covers the essentials
at a lower price and a smaller storage footprint. If 1,152Wh feels tight for a CPAP or a small
off-grid fridge on longer stints, Bluetti’s own AC180P bumps
capacity to 1,440Wh — and is actually a few pounds lighter — for about $100-150 more.
 5. Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 — Best for Boondocking + Solar
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 (2,042Wh)
 Best for boondocking + solar · ~$799 ($1,499 MSRP) · 2,042Wh LiFePO4 · 2,200W AC
 Pairs cleanly with Jackery SolarSaga panels for a straightforward, no-fuss off-grid recharge setup.
 2,200W continuous, 4,400W surge, and a simple display/app that's easy to hand off to anyone in the rig.
 Recharges to 80% from a wall outlet in about two hours when you do have shore power available.
 For boondockers who want to lean on solar rather than shore power or a generator, the Explorer 2000 v2’s
straightforward panel pairing and simple interface make it the easiest unit here to run entirely
off-grid without a learning curve. See our full Jackery Explorer 2000 v2
review for a deeper look at the trade-offs.
 How to size a power station for your RV
 List your actual off-grid loads: lights, water pump, fridge, device charging, and maybe a CPAP or microwave — rooftop AC is a separate conversation (see above).
 Match continuous watts to your heaviest load, not just capacity: a 2,000Wh unit with a 1,800W inverter still can’t run a microwave and a fridge compressor cycling at the same moment.
 Plan your recharge path: shore power at a campground, solar while boondocking, or your tow vehicle’s 12V outlet while driving — the best RV units support all three.
 Buy into an expandable line if you’re not sure: the Delta 2 Max, Delta Pro, and F2000 all take add-on batteries, so you can start smaller and grow.
 Rooftop AC needs a soft-start device, not just a bigger battery: even a large power station usually can’t handle the starting surge without one.
 For a lighter, grab-and-go unit for tent camping instead, see our
 best portable power station for camping picks, or
compare full solar-and-battery kits in our
 best solar generator roundup. Boondocking off solar rather than shore
power? Our best foldable solar panel picks break down which
wattage class actually recharges an RV-size battery in a day. Sizing a unit for a fixed home setup
instead of a rig? Our power station sizing guide breaks
the watt-hour math down device by device. Once you’ve picked one, our power station maintenance
guide covers the storage and temperature habits that matter most
for a unit that lives in an RV’s temperature swings.
 The bottom line
 The EcoFlow Delta 2 Max is the best RV power station for most rigs — compact, flexible about how
it recharges, and sized right for the loads most RVers actually run off-grid. Full-time RVers or
anyone chasing rooftop AC support should size up to the EcoFlow Delta Pro , the Anker SOLIX F2000 
is the safest expandable buy if you’re not sure how much capacity you’ll need, the Bluetti AC180 
covers smaller rigs and tighter budgets, and the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is the easiest to run
purely on solar for boondocking-heavy trips.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What's the best power station for an RV in 2026? The EcoFlow Delta 2 Max is the best all-around RV power station — a 2,048Wh LiFePO4 unit with 2,400W continuous output (3,400W with X-Boost) that's compact enough for a cabinet or under-bed storage bay, expandable if you need more capacity, and fast enough on solar or shore power to recharge between travel days. Full-time RVers who want to run heavier appliances should look at the larger EcoFlow Delta Pro instead.
 Can a portable power station run my RV's rooftop air conditioner? Not directly in most cases. A typical 13,500 BTU RV rooftop AC needs a surge of roughly 2,800-3,500 starting watts, more than all but the largest power stations can deliver on their own. Adding a soft-start device like a Micro-Air EasyStart, which cuts that starting surge by up to 70%, is what lets larger units like the EcoFlow Delta Pro or Anker SOLIX F3800 run rooftop AC off battery power.
 How much power station capacity does an RV actually need? For a weekend boondocking trip running lights, a fridge, water pump, and device charging, 1,000-2,000Wh is usually enough. Full-time RVers or anyone running a CPAP, microwave, or rooftop AC should plan for 2,000-3,600Wh with expansion batteries, plus solar panels to recharge without shore power or a generator.

 Power stations are ideal for helping you get through a power outage and for off-grid camping. They offer a compelling alternative to loud and smelly generators. And, unlike gas generators, power stations don't emit potentially lethal carbon monoxide fumes and can be recharged with optional solar panels . 
 The Jackery 2000 v2 is the best power station for those who need additional power for multi-day off-grid camping, or for an extended blackout. Recently reduced in price, it can now be found for under $900 on Amazon. At 39 lbs, it is light enough that most people will find it easy to pack and move around, and it is easy to add optional solar recharging. It's our favorite option for extended off-grid camping.

It delivers on most people's basic needs, such as getting through a blackout in comfort, providing power for an off-grid camping trip, or offering portable power away from a 110V outlet. Affordably priced — currently on sale for under $530 — it offers a combination of price, power, and portability that hits the sweet spot: ample power without breaking the bank. 
 If your primary goal is home backup power, step up to the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 . It is designed specifically for home backup power use, and can be wired directly into your home breaker panel with an optional transfer switch kit. Its 4,000-watt output and 4,096 Wh capacity allow for high-wattage appliance use and extended blackout capability. With expansion options up to 48 kWh, the Delta Pro 3 is a great starting point for those looking to transition to full home backup power. It also supports up to 2,600 watts of solar charging, allowing you to utilize solar in van builds and off-grid home use. EcoFlow makes an optional Transfer Switch Kit that makes it easy and fast to use the Delta Pro 3 to power your essential home circuits during a blackout. As our tester notes, “ the Delta Pro 3's ample power and battery expansion potential made it my go-to choice to build out my home backup setup .”

 How We Tested
 Our testing process for power stations is extensive. We subject each product to hundreds of hours of hands-on use and testing to evaluate power output, runtime, device compatibility, and ease of operation. 
 We do not rely on manufacturer claims or specifications to determine things like each product's actual usable AC power output. We use sophisticated power measurement equipment, along with some creative test jigs of our own custom design, to stress test each product and measure its real-world capabilities. 
 None of the products we tested actually delivers usable AC power output that matches their claimed capacity . For example, a 2,000 watt-hour power station will not provide you with 2,000 watt-hours of usable AC power — only 60% to 93% of the claimed capacity is actually delivered and usable to power your devices through the AC outlets. Since products vary so widely in the actual usable power they deliver, we consider the usable AC power output to be the single most important information to help guide your purchase decision-making. 
 We use precision power measurement equipment to measure runtime and charging speeds. You can learn more about our power station testing protocol and process, in our How We Test article. 
Our tests inform our rating scores, which reflect the four key factors we believe are most important for you to make a smarter purchase decision:

 Why Trust GearLab
 Our power station test team have a combined 20 years of experience using power stations in conditions ranging from power outages to off-grid camping to remote tool use. Our review team includes experts in electronics, off-grid power and solar charging, and consumer-electronics review and testing. 
 GearLab co-founder RJ Spurrier , a Robotics Engineer educated at UC Berkeley's Engineering school, has been using power stations for more than 15 years, starting from the time he organized an off-grid movie night with friends on San Francisco's Ocean Beach. Today, RJ is a dedicated off-grid camper with his family, using solar panels and power stations to enable extended outdoor adventures across the mountains and deserts of the US West. RJ also uses power station batteries and solar panels to power his net-zero home , which combines a 45-panel solar array with a 20 kWh power station system for home backup.
 Senior Research Analyst, Sentry Kelly boasts a formal education in Applied Manufacturing Engineering, Sentry has the knowledge and training to analyze just about any mechanical or electrical product out there. In his free time, Sentry and his wife travel far and wide in his custom-built van that is outfitted with solar panels and a power station as the primary power source for their extended off-grid camping adventures. 
 Research Analyst Kenji Mowrey leads our field testing of each power station. Kenji earned his bachelor's degree in Outdoor Product Design from Oregon State and has a lifelong passion and curiosity for discovering what separates good consumer products from the great ones. Kenji blends his analytical and science-based testing with a pursuit of electronics and outdoor equipment that are simply a joy to use, never let you down, and work just as expected.

 What's the Best Value?
 The Jackery 300 is the winner of our Best Buy award because it is small, affordable, and a great solution for keeping your phone and laptop recharged. However, it won't be a great value if your goal is to power higher-wattage devices or appliances — for example, you can't power a space heater, stove burner, or even a hot water kettle with the Jackery 300. 
 Figure out how much power you need . From our perspective, the best value strategy for power stations is to focus on what you want to power and avoid overspending on more capacity than you actually need. 
 Choosing the right power station is largely determined by your power needs. To save money, first figure out how much power you need, then pick the best device that meets your needs.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 While it is tempting to jump to higher power output, keep in mind that doubling power capacity will double the cost (and the weight). It might not be worth it. (Although we admittedly find ourselves wanting more power now for off-grid camping than we did in the past.)
 Adding Solar Can Save You Money 
A 2,000 Wh power station like the Jackery 2000 v2 might be all the power you need for a weekend camping trip. But you are unlikely to get 5-7 days of off-grid camping power out of it. Going to a 4,000 Wh power station could solve that problem, but it will cost you another $1,000 . A more economical solution? Consider adding a 200 watt solar panel for less than $400 , which might extend your runtime for days.
 The good news is costs are coming down . Unlike most consumer electronics categories, power stations and solar panels have become much more affordable over the last few years. In 2024, each 1,000 Wh of power station capacity would cost you about $1,000, or $1/Wh. Today, many of the most compelling power station products can be found for less than half that cost — around $0.40/Wh.

 How to Choose A Power Station
 Before deciding which power station will be right for you, there are a few key factors to consider. Below are some key questions that summarize key points from our buying advice article.
 An electric cooler is very convenient for camping. But, be sure to bring it to a cool temperature at home or when plugged into your car 12v plug while driving, since the initial cooling is when it draws the most power.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 How Much Power Do I Need? 
 Power stations are more limited in the maximum AC wattage and runtime they can provide, which is intuitively obvious. We are all accustomed to plugging in whatever we want into an AC outlet, and it just works. But, off-grid camping power or managing through a multi-day blackout requires planning about what kinds of devices you run to avoid fully depleting your power station prematurely. Dialing in your power station requirements takes discipline: you may need to pull back from what you want , to think about what you really need . 
 The Power Output section above includes some tables to help you determine what power station capacity will best meet your requirements.
 Note that certain kinds of devices, like space heaters, cooking appliances, and charging ebikes, are much more demanding of power than most other common devices. If you desire to run these higher-power devices, you'll want to calculate your power needs more carefully to ensure you have capacity for the runtime you need. 
 For multi-day power needs, adding optional solar panels may be helpful. Read on below for more info on solar panels.
One of our Editors has invested in a large-scale solar panel system for his home, with 45 solar panels on his roof, and an integrated power station battery capacity of 20 kWh. He notes, “ Our home puts more power into the grid each year than we use, and the power station batteries allow us to pull power when needed during lower-rate cost times of the day. And, we push power onto the grid in the summer during the highest rate for reimbursement times of day. ” Yet, even with that large-scale home backup system, it does not provide enough power for a 24-hour power outage during winter unless he turns off the breakers for all non-essential circuits. The reality is that providing the daily power most on-grid homeowners are accustomed to is beyond the capability of most solar + power station systems.
 What's Your Favorite Electric Gear for Off-grid Camping? 
 We are unabashed fans of electric camping . It can take a yeoman camping trip in the middle of nowhere and turn it into a magical romantic experience or a family fun adventure everyone will remember for years to come. Here's a list of some of our favorite gear and their power requirements:
 LED String Lights — ok, we've got to start with this, because whether it is romance, or a magical family experience, it is all about the lighting . For less than $20 for our best buy winner in string lights , which consumes less than 30 watts of power, you can dress up your campsite with 25 warm glowing LED lights. Oooh. So nice. We love it! And, learn how to play guitar too (acoustic, please) for the full monte. 
 Electric Cooler — we started reviewing electric coolers years ago, but only recently have they become truly awesome. Skip that stop at the store to buy ice, skip all the space taken by the ice, and eliminate the yucky pool of melted water getting in your food on Sunday morning — welcome to the new core tool for camping: the electric cooler. It is a game changer. Pro tip: extend your power station runtime by cooling down your electric cooler using AC power at home, or on the drive plugged into your car 12v plug --it is when cooling down that a powered cooler requires the most electricity. 
 Outdoor Projector — yeah, that is a thing too. Family camping experience: check! Remote location: check! Pixar movie at your campsite: coolest parents ever ! But, do have your power station handy and not fully drained. A quality outdoor projector like the XGIMI Halo+ is a great choice and has its own battery, but if that battery runs out 10 mins before the movie ends, you will go from coolest parents ever to a total meltdown — the power station might save the day (and let you watch more than one movie too)! 
 LED Lanterns — while there may be some who have nostalgia for old-school kerosene or white gas mantel lanterns, at GearLab we love modern LED Lanterns for safe and quiet task lighting when preparing meals. Even if you have a full set of LED String lights, it is great to have a bright rechargeable LED Lantern (or two) when preparing meals or putting a band-aid on a kiddo. 
 Induction Electric Burner — not everyone is ready to give up their old-school fuel-based Coleman camping stove, but we think they are going away in the future too. The full electric camping experience embraces an induction burner (1800W) to replace old-school propane and white gas camping stoves (note you'll need induction-compatible pots and pans to go with it). An induction burner is safer when camping with kids, more efficient with power usage than an old-school electric burner, and you'll rid yourself of the fuel, the fumes, and the fire risks associated with an old-school fuel camping stove . 
 Electric Kettle — boiling water is a recurring task when camping, whether it's for coffee, tea, oatmeal, hot chocolate, or instant “ just-add-water ” foods. A basic electric kettle (1500W) just makes it so easy and fast. 
 Electric Griddle — Another slick addition to your electric camping dream set-up is an electric griddle (1500W). They are great for cooking pancakes, eggs, grilled cheese sandwiches, bacon, sausage links, and more. 
Keep in mind the power you'll need, which adds up fast. You'll want at least a 2,000 Wh power station, and one with at least 2,000 AC watt support. The cooking devices are high AC Watt so you'll need to run them one at a time unless you buy a higher capacity power station. We love having all three — a kettle , an induction burner , and a griddle — but if space is tight, a burner alone will do. Adding one or two 200 watt solar panels will greatly extend your battery runtime by recharging your power station on sunny days.
 Are Solar Panel(s) a Must-have for a Power Station? 
 No. Many people do not need to invest in solar panels for their power station . The only reason to consider a solar panel is if you need more power over multiple days than your power station can provide. For most people, a suitable power station, like the Jackery 2000 v2 will provide you with adequate power for comfort during a multi-hour blackout and/or a typical weekend camping trip. Obtaining a 12v car adapter charging cable for your power station is a low-cost way to recharge anytime you use your vehicle when camping. 
 In our experience, it is when you need support for 3 or more days without grid power that a solar panel becomes a necessity. 
 A 3-day weekend off-grid camping trip can easily drain your power station and leave you with no power halfway into your trip. 
For example, we recently did a 3-day family camping trip in the Sierra Nevada mountain range using the Jackery 2000 v2. Our off-grid campsite included amenities such as LED string lights, an electric cooler, an inductive stove, two ebikes, recharging phones and iPads, and a SpaceX Starlink system. That camp setup draws too much power each day to make it through a 3-day trip. But, by using two 200 watt solar panels, we were able to fully charge up each day. One tester said, “ It was liberating to camp off-grid, in the middle of nowhere, and with such a cool camp setup. My family had a blast! In fact, we had plenty of power to be out there for a week or more of off-grid camping, so long as the sun kept shining .”

It works well for small tasks like charging devices and running small appliances, but there are more compelling options in the 200-300 Wh class. 
 Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus — The 5000 Plus sports a 5040 Wh capacity, ideal for powering large home appliances during blackouts, with 240V outlet configurations and expansion options capable of supplying multiple days of backup power. A power station this size is a significant investment and is most practical when integrated with your home's circuits via a transfer switch kit, along with solar panels and additional battery packs, which quickly increases the cost and benefit of owning a power station over a gas generator. 
 Jackery Explorer 500 — The Jackery Explorer 500 shares many of the same qualities as the smaller Jackery 300 but with a bigger battery capacity and higher power output. Though it takes over 5 hours to recharge via a standard wall outlet and has only a single AC port, making it less practical for anything beyond charging phones and laptops. 
 Goal Zero Yeti 500 — The Yeti 500 is a 499 Wh power station that weighs 16 lbs and produces 500 watts of power output. The Yeti 500 has enough power to run some appliances, such as a CPAP machine, but is underpowered for larger items like coffee makers and induction cooktops. Given the limited ports, like only having 2 AC outlets and just one 60 watt USb-C port, there are more enticing options available in the 500 Wh category. 
 DJI Power 2000 — The Power 2000 is DJI's debut in the power station market. It's large enough to cover multiple days of camping or keep an appliance or two charged during an outage. It has a couple of enticing features, such as a 30A RV plug and eight USB-C/USB-A ports. However, the proprietary charging ports are disappointing; you'll need to purchase additional accessories for solar or car charging, quickly making the 2000 an expensive option, especially compared to almost every competitor that has built-in solar and car charging ports. 
 EcoFlow Delta 3 Max — The Delta 3 Max is a beefed up version of the popular EcoFlow Delta 3 . It has double the battery capacity at 2048 Wh and a power output of 2400 watts. The tradeoff is that it weighs 44 lbs and costs a few hundred dollars more than the Delta 3. If you like the Delta lineup but need a bit more capability and battery storage, the Delta 3 Max is worth considering. 
 Anker Solix F3800 — The F3800 is a large, home backup power station that serves as a starting point for building out a full-scale home backup system. It has expandability up to 53.8 kWh, enough to power your home for multiple days during outages. The dual 120V/240V outlet opens up more appliance options, such as clothes dryers and electric ranges, and it also directly supports EV charging via the NEMA 14-50 port. Like any other large, home backup power station, the F3800 is a significant investment and is difficult to transport or move. 
 Conclusion
 Our breakdown of portable power stations aims to simplify the confusing and continually evolving information involved in purchasing one. After months of extensive testing and research, we hope our portable power station review provides the necessary knowledge and guidance to help you make an informed decision about your power needs.
 The right portable power station can help supplement your power needs, whether you're on the road, at home, or anywhere in between.   Credit: Kenji Mowrey

 Battery capacity 
Power station battery capacity is measured in Watt Hours (Wh) - or 1 watt of energy used per hour. The higher the number, the more battery capacity the unit has, the longer it lasts without requiring a recharge. To give you an idea of the power a unit has, an iPhone 17 Pro Max has a battery capacity of 20Wh; the cheapest and smallest portable power station in this guide has a capacity of 245Wh.
 Output 
Output measures the total continuous power supply a unit can deliver, and is measured in Watts (W). Small devices like a laptop and coolers tends to need around 60 to 100W of continuous power whereas appliances like fridges can need up to around 800W. So, a large portable power station with a higher output is best for powering large devices, or more devices at once.
 Input 
Portable power stations are usually charged via the mains - it's quick and efficient, especially for higher-capacity units. Many also let you charge the device from the car using a 12V cigarette lighter socket - ideal for those living the van life or in the RV. You can recharge some devices using solar panels, too.
 Solar 
Every portable power station I've selected for this guide have solar charging capabilities for off-grid power supply, but not every unit you can buy does. The solar panels can come bundled with the unit or bought separately. Smaller power stations will have a lower maximum solar input, making them slower to charge.
 UPS 
Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) is essential for ensuring reliable and continuous power even during black-outs. If you're using your unit for devices like routers or fridges, it's. Effectively, a UPS-enabled power station will step in during a power outage to continue charging or powering connected devices. Times vary, and while we're talking a matter of milliseconds, if it's a 'mission-critical' device, then select one with a faster switchover time.
 High surge wattage 
 This is especially important if you're using a portable power station on a job-site, as some tools, like circular saws, draw a huge amount of power at once. So, a unit with a high surge wattage (or high surge rating) prevents the machinery from tripping out the unit.
 Size & weight 
"Portable" isn't one size fits all. My team and I have reviewed everything from compact and handheld units to massive power stations that have built in wheels or need a trolley to move them. Depending on how and where you'll be using the unit, you'll want check the dimensions. As you'd expect, the higher the battery capacity, the heavier the power station will be.
 Ports 
Port selection is always worth checking. Portable power stations almost always include USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as mains outlets. However, larger units will usually have a higher number of ports as there's extra space for them, and the unit holds more power to charge more devices. Some go beyond this - for example, DJI's products include an SDC port for charging DJI drones on the go.
 Best portable power stations: FAQs 
 Are portable power stations worth it?
 Yes, but it depends on how often you use it and how many devices you're charging. There are a lot of models on the market, and the best portable power stations can handle everything from charging mobile devices and laptops to powering appliances and even EVs. If your needs are simple, you can pick up a good portable power station for around $200.
If you like going to campsites that have a power hookup they're not worth it as connecting to mains doesn't cost that much compared to a power station. For longer periods off-grid a generator is still, for me, the better option but for short weekend trips where you cannot get a power source these can completely change the weekend for the better if you want to keep using your tech or use electric-powered camping gadgets.
 What is the difference between a portable power station and a generator?
 Generally speaking, a portable power station is charged and outputs electricity. Generators tend to refer to units that use fuel like gasoline to generate energy and power. 
 Both can be used for back-up purposes, and both have different pros and cons. 
 Power stations are quieter, cleaner and more eco-friendly. However, their battery capacity can be low, and if it runs out of charge during a power-cut, you'd best hope it has built-in solar panels to re-charge. 
 Power generators are ideal for running heavy appliances, as they have a higher capacity, and isn't reliant on electricity, making it perfect for a back-up solution. 
 How many years do portable power stations last?
 A portable power station's lifespan depends on usage frequency and battery chemistry, but most last between 5 and 10 years with regular use. Like a phone or laptop battery, its capacity gradually degrades over time until it can no longer hold a full charge.
 THere are several key factors influence a portable power station's longevity: 
 The first is the battery type; models with Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries often last up to 10 years (3,000+ full charge cycles), while standard Lithium-ion (NMC) models usually last 3 to 5 years (500 to 1,000 cycles) before capacity drops to 80%. 
 The second and third factors, which we've combines, depends on a station's usage and storage; frequent deep discharges, exposure to extreme temperatures, and storing the unit fully empty accelerate battery degradation all affect its lifespan.
 How many Watt Hours do I need?
 Start by listing every device or appliance you want to power. For anything you'll run continuously — a fridge, a router, a lamp — multiply its wattage by the number of hours you need it running. For devices you'll charge and then use, like a phone or laptop, find the battery capacity in Wh (usually on the device label or manufacturer's website) and multiply that by the number of times you want to charge it.
 Add all those figures together and that's your minimum capacity requirement.
 It's worth adding a 20–30% buffer on top of that figure. Real-world capacity is affected by temperature, battery age, and the startup surge that motors and compressors draw when they first switch on.
 What can you run on a portable power station?
 So long as your portable power station has the right ports and enough capacity, it can run a massive range of devices, including phones, laptops, and desktops. 
 Higher capacity units will also let you power large home appliances and charge electric vehicles. 
 Check which ports your preferred model has, including USB Type-A and Type-C, AC and mains sockets.
 How long can you run a portable power station?
 It all depends on the power station and the device or devices you're charging. As a general rule of thumb, to figure out how long your portable power station can run, divide battery capacity (Wh) by power drawn by the device (W). 
 What is UPS and why do I need it?
 UPS stands for Uninterrupted Power Supply, and it’s a really important feature if you’re powering devices like routers and household appliances like fridges, or working on-site and need reliability. If you experience a power outage, the portable power station will automatically and seamlessly continue charge your devices without dropping the supply. 
 How we test the best portable power stations 
 Our team of expert reviewers have hand-tested a range of outdoor-ready equipment, including the best rugged smartphones , the best rugged laptops , and the best rugged tablets for working out in the field. We've even tested out the best rugged hard drives . So, we know what to look for when it comes to technology for rural locations and hostile environments.
 We test the best portable power stations on volume, weight, battery chemistry, and additional feature sets. Before writing any review, we try to fully understand the unit to describe each device's pros and cons best and accurately compare them. Part of this process is through benchmark tests, part is through daily use, and part is through simulated or real scenarios.
 As the main function of these devices is to be batteries, we test charge and discharge cycles on every unit. First and foremost, this is the most important feature of the portable power stations we test. If they cannot meet our standard here or do not come near what the other portable power stations in this guide are capable of, we will most likely not include them.
 Next, we push the power stations to their limits and beyond. We intentionally exceed the maximum power allowed on each generator, then observe and note the recovery from the over-power protection. This helps us promote safe power stations for you and your family.
 To ensure reliability, these tests are designed to learn the features, the downfalls, and the limits of the power stations tested by our subject matter experts.

 Research-backed What we'd buy today 
 Compare portable power stations for RV travel, boondocking, and campsite backup using capacity, output, charging speed, and real-world fit.
 If we were buying a new portable power station for RV travel today, we would start with the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2. It combines a useful 1,024Wh battery, 2,000W continuous AC output, a 24.9-pound carry weight, and very fast wall charging in a size that still belongs in the word “portable.”
 That does not make it the automatic answer for every rig. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus is more flexible if you want battery expansion and unusually strong solar input. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is lighter and straightforward. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 makes a compelling value case while retaining 1,800W output and high solar input.
 This guide explains how we reached those conclusions, what each unit does best, and how to size a power station around the equipment you actually plan to run.

We reviewed current manufacturer specifications, independent testing, warranty and support information, and RV-specific tradeoffs.  If we could buy one today
 We would choose the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 for a general-purpose RV and road-trip power station. Its 2,000W output creates more room for demanding appliances than the Jackery, while its 24.9-pound weight is noticeably easier to move than many units in this class. Anker advertises a full AC recharge in 49 minutes when UltraFast mode is enabled in the app.
 Independent lab testing supports the portability case: OutdoorGearLab praised its power-to-weight combination and suitability for weight-conscious travelers. The compromise is important: Anker says the Gen 2 does not accept an expansion battery . If we expected the system to grow beyond 1kWh, we would buy the EcoFlow instead.

 How we chose these four
 We focused on the 1kWh class because it is a practical middle ground for many RV travelers. These units can handle electronics, lighting, fans, a portable refrigerator or cooler, and many small appliances without becoming a 70-pound system that rarely leaves the storage bay.
 Every finalist had to meet the following screen:
 Current LiFePO4 battery chemistry with a published long-cycle-life claim
 Roughly 1,000Wh of capacity and at least 1,500W of continuous AC output
 A weight that one capable adult can reasonably move
 AC, solar, and vehicle-charging options
 A known manufacturer with published product support and warranty information
 Enough independent testing or established owner feedback to look beyond the sales page
 We did not rank temporary sale prices because they can change between reading and checkout. Instead, the value pick is the model that becomes most attractive when its real checkout price is substantially lower without giving up the features your trip requires.
 1. Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: our all-around pick
 The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is the most balanced answer here. Its 1,024Wh LFP battery feeds a 2,000W continuous inverter with 3,000W peak output across 10 ports. Anker lists 4,000 cycles before the battery reaches at least 80% capacity, a 10-millisecond UPS switchover, 600W maximum solar input, and a 49-minute full AC charge through its app-enabled UltraFast mode.
 For an RV traveler, the headline is not the record-style charging claim. It is the combination of 2,000W output and 24.9-pound weight. That is enough inverter headroom for many coffee makers, microwaves, induction burners, and other short-duration appliances—provided the appliance’s actual running and startup demand remains within the unit’s limits.
 Choose it if
 You want one portable unit for campsite, vehicle, and home-outage duty.
 Fast shore-power or household-outlet charging matters.
 You will move it often and still want 2,000W continuous output.
 One kilowatt-hour is enough for the way you camp.
 Skip it if
 You want to add a matching expansion battery later. Anker’s support documentation says the Gen 2 omits expansion to reduce size and weight. It also should not be treated as weatherproof simply because it is camping equipment; follow the storage and operating limits in the manual.
 2. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: best for a system that can grow
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus pairs a 1,024Wh LFP battery with 1,800W continuous output, 3,600W surge output, 13 output ports, two USB-C ports rated up to 140W, and two solar inputs that accept up to 500W each.
 EcoFlow says it can expand with compatible batteries to as much as 5kWh. That changes the purchase from a self-contained box into the beginning of a larger power system. It also supports EcoFlow’s 800W alternator charger, which can matter more than portable solar for travelers who regularly move between camps.
 At about 27.6 pounds, it is still portable but is the heaviest of these four. The dual solar inputs and expansion path are wasted if the unit will only charge from a campground pedestal and power phones. They become valuable when longer off-grid stays are genuinely part of the plan.
 Choose it if

 High solar input or an alternator-charging ecosystem matters.
 You need many simultaneous ports or high-output USB-C charging.
 Skip it if
 You only need a compact weekend box and will never buy the extra battery, solar array, or alternator charger that creates its advantage.

 3. Jackery Explorer 1000 v2: best for uncomplicated portability
 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 offers the largest battery in this comparison at 1,070Wh while weighing about 23.8 pounds. It provides 1,500W continuous output, 3,000W surge, three AC outlets, two USB-C ports, one USB-A port, a 12V vehicle port, and up to 400W of solar input.
 Its advantage is easy to understand: it is the lightest choice here and its interface is approachable. TechRadar’s current portable-power roundup highlights the Explorer 1000 v2 for camping and praises the updated model’s portability and port selection. The tradeoff is the lowest continuous AC output in the group.
 That 1,500W limit is not a problem for laptops, camera batteries, lighting, fans, many portable fridges, and modest appliances. It becomes the deciding limitation when a traveler wants to run a higher-wattage cooker, heater, microwave, or other equipment with demanding startup current.

 The unit will be carried between home, RV, picnic table, or tent regularly.
 Your device list stays comfortably below 1,500W.
 You value a simple, established product line over maximum configurability.

 This is the one we would price-check against the Anker before checkout. If it is meaningfully less expensive and 1,800W is enough, it can be the smarter value. Its 1,000W solar ceiling is especially appealing on paper, although realizing that input requires a sizable, compatible array and strong conditions.

 The current price is substantially below the Anker or EcoFlow.

 How to size a portable power station for your RV
 Use your own daily loads
 Build an RV power budget before you choose a model
 Our free calculator turns running watts, operating hours, reserve, efficiency, and days between recharges into a practical capacity estimate.
 Use the RV power station size calculator 
 Start with the appliance, not the battery. Read the device label or measure the actual running wattage with an appropriate power meter. Multiply watts by the hours you expect to run it, then add a practical reserve for inverter losses, standby use, changing temperatures, and the fact that estimates are never exact.
 For example, a device averaging 60W for eight hours consumes about 480Wh before losses. A 1,024Wh station should not be described as “17 hours guaranteed,” because the inverter, other loads, cycling behavior, and conditions all affect the result. Planning on 20–25% reserve is more realistic than spending every advertised watt-hour on paper.
 Then confirm four separate limits:
 Continuous watts: what the inverter can provide steadily.
 Starting or surge watts: the brief demand when a compressor or motor starts.
 Watt-hours: the energy available over time.
 Recharge rate: how quickly AC, solar, or vehicle charging can put that energy back.
 A high-watt inverter does not create more runtime. A large battery does not guarantee it can start a demanding appliance. Both sides of the equation have to work.
 RV connection and safety realities
 Do not backfeed an RV, house, or electrical panel through an improvised cord. Use only manufacturer-approved connections and a properly designed transfer method.
 A portable station’s 120V outlet does not magically provide full 30A or 50A RV service. Any adapter still leaves the system limited by the power station’s inverter, outlet, and cable ratings.
 Keep the station dry, ventilated, secured for travel, and away from heat sources. Follow its charging and operating-temperature limits.
 Confirm whether the 12V outlet is regulated if a refrigerator or other device is sensitive to voltage changes.
 For CPAP, oxygen, or another important medical device, confirm compatibility and backup planning with the device manufacturer and healthcare professional; do not rely on a casual runtime estimate.
 Check the CPSC recall database and the manufacturer’s recall page for the exact model before buying used or discounted inventory.
 Questions to answer before checkout
 Which exact devices must it run, and what are their measured running and startup watts?
 How many watt-hours does a normal day consume?
 Will it recharge from campground power, home AC, solar, an alternator charger, or a mix?
 Can you lift it safely and secure it in the available storage space?
 Do you need expansion later, or is portability the reason to stay near 1kWh?
 Are the required solar cables, adapters, panels, and vehicle-charging parts included?
 What warranty applies to the actual seller, country, and purchase channel?
 Portable power station FAQs
 Can a 1kWh power station run an RV air conditioner?
 Sometimes briefly, but this is not a safe blanket promise. The air conditioner’s running wattage, compressor startup surge, soft-start equipment, outside temperature, and every other active load matter. Even when the inverter can start it, a 1kWh battery may provide disappointing runtime.
 Can I plug my RV into one of these power stations?
 Some travelers use a correctly rated adapter for limited RV loads, but the power station’s inverter and outlet remain the limit—not the number printed on the RV plug. Turn off high-demand loads and follow both manufacturers’ instructions. Never improvise a backfeed connection.
 Is a portable power station the same as a generator?
 No. A portable power station stores electrical energy in a battery and must be recharged. A fuel generator creates electricity while fuel is available. Battery stations are quiet and have no combustion exhaust, but they provide finite stored energy.
 How much solar panel capacity do I need?
 Start with daily energy use and the hours of productive sun you can realistically expect. A power station’s maximum solar-input rating is only the ceiling. Weather, shade, panel angle, temperature, cabling, and controller limits reduce real production.
 Should I buy the power station or a solar bundle?
 Buy the bundle only when the panel voltage and connector match, the panel will fit and be deployed regularly, and the bundle price is better than suitable alternatives. For campground-heavy travel, a panel may spend most of its life in storage.
 The Green Machine verdict
 If we were buying today, we would choose the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 for most RV travel. We would switch to the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus when expandability or 1,000W solar input mattered more, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 when the easiest carry mattered most, or the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 when a strong sale made it the clear value.
 The best choice is the smallest system that comfortably runs the actual plan and can be recharged before the next time it is needed.  Buying and setup checklist
 Write down the highest running wattage and startup surge of every intended appliance.
 Choose at least the required continuous and peak inverter ratings, not just the largest Wh number.
 Estimate daily Wh, then add margin for conversion loss, cold temperatures and battery reserve.
 Confirm weight, dimensions and handle ergonomics for the distance you will carry it.
 Check solar wattage, voltage range, connector type and whether panels are included.
 Verify UPS transfer behavior on the exact outlets you plan to use.
 Read warranty terms and regional service conditions.
 Test the complete load before an outage or trip.
 Store the station according to the manual, away from moisture and extreme heat, and recharge it periodically.
 Common mistakes and fixes
 Buying by watt-hours alone
 Symptom: the battery has plenty of capacity but the kettle, compressor or tool will not start. Fix: compare continuous and peak AC ratings and measure startup demand.
 Assuming a “UPS” label guarantees every device will stay online
 Symptom: a router or computer reboots during a test. Fix: enable the correct UPS mode, update firmware, use the specified outlet group and test with the real load.
 Expecting the advertised refrigerator hours in every outage
 Symptom: runtime is much shorter than the headline claim. Fix: measure the refrigerator’s duty cycle, keep the door closed, remove other loads and account for temperature and conversion losses.
 Overloading the solar input
 Symptom: charging stops or an input warning appears. Fix: stay within the station’s voltage, current and wattage limits and use compatible cables.
 Ignoring transport and ventilation
 Symptom: the unit is impractical to move or its fan runs constantly. Fix: verify weight and handles before buying, then operate it in a shaded, ventilated location with clear vents.
 Verdict
 For most people spending less than $1,000, the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 is the sensible portable starting point: enough inverter power for many everyday devices, a 1,070Wh LiFePO4 battery and a reported $519 price.  How many watt-hours do you actually need?
Start from the load, not the product page. Add up what each device draws and how many hours a
 day it genuinely runs, and you will usually land somewhere between 400 and 900 watt-hours a day.
 A 45 quart compressor fridge is the anchor: it draws roughly 30 to 45 amp-hours a day at 90F
 ambient, which is 400 to 550 watt-hours once you multiply by nominal voltage. Lights add 100 to
 200 watt-hours. A laptop is 50 to 60 watt-hours per charge, and phones are noise by comparison.
To convert a station's rating into the amp-hour language the rest of a 12V build speaks, divide
 watt-hours by 12.8 , the nominal voltage of a LiFePO4 pack. The
 Delta 3 Plus at 1024Wh is therefore roughly 80Ah , which is very close
 to what a 100Ah lithium house battery actually gives you at a sensible depth of discharge. That
 equivalence is the single most useful number on this page, because it lets you compare a sealed
 station against a DIY bank without arguing about marketing units.
Then apply the rule that saves people from buying twice: size for the days you will not charge,
 not the days you will. If you drive every day and have a roof array, one kilowatt-hour is
 generous. If your pattern is to park at a trailhead on a Friday and not move until Sunday
 afternoon, in trees, you need double. Work your own figure with the
 power consumption calculator before you
 read another spec sheet.

Capacity and inverter figures are the manufacturers' published specifications. Amp-hours are
 watt-hours divided by 12.8. Fridge days assume a 45 quart compressor fridge using 500 watt-hours
 a day in warm weather and nothing else drawing from the pack, so treat them as a ceiling rather
 than a plan. Budgets are bands; check the current price on Amazon before ordering.
 Which portable power station should most overlanders buy?
The Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at under $1,000. The case is
 arithmetic rather than brand. Apply this page's own sizing rule, size for the days you will not
 charge, and a 1kWh unit gives you about two fridge days while the Elite gives you
4.1. It does that at about 50 percent less per watt-hour than the
1,024Wh Delta 3 Plus at under $1,000, so
 the extra days cost nothing extra. Its 2,600W inverter is the largest in the 2kWh
 class here, and the maker rates the cells to 4,000 cycles.
It also accepts up to 1,000W of solar input, and that number matters more
 than it looks. A station that caps solar at 200W can never quite keep up with a fridge plus
 incidentals on a cloudy day, so you slowly drain over a week. With a high ceiling, two
 Renogy 200W panels plus a portable return
 more than a full day of load on a clear day by the arithmetic further down this page. Match the
 array to the input ceiling with the
 solar array calculator rather than buying
 panels the station cannot use.
The price of all that is weight. At 53.6 lb it is more than twice the
23.8 lb Jackery, and it is a unit you strap down and leave in the vehicle
 rather than one you carry to a picnic table. If that is a deal breaker, the honest 1kWh
 alternatives are the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at
under $500, the lightest 1kWh LiFePO4 unit here, and the
 Bluetti AC180 at under $500, which has the most
 capacity of the 1kWh class, a well regarded UPS mode and the lowest cost per watt-hour on this page. Pick the Jackery if the station moves between
 vehicle and camp, the AC180 if it lives in a cabinet and never moves again.
The EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus is still a sound unit,
 and it remains the answer for one specific buyer: someone who wants a small station now and
 intends to add EcoFlow expansion batteries later. At under $1,000 it is no longer the
 default, because the same money now buys twice the capacity on day one.
 What does the beginner tier actually get you?
The entry tier here is not a compromised version of the middle tier, it is a different length of
 trip. The EcoFlow River 3 Max Plus at under $500
holds 858 watt-hours, which is roughly 67 amp-hours, and that runs a small fridge for a long
 weekend without the anxious battery check at 6am. It will not run a hair dryer, a microwave or
 an induction burner, because its inverter tops out at 990W.
The Anker SOLIX C1000 at under $500 is the
 best capacity per dollar in the entry tier: a full kilowatt-hour with an 1800W inverter at
about 10 percent less per watt-hour than the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2. Its 58 minute AC recharge sounds like marketing until
 your only charging window is a two hour drive between camps and a coffee stop with an outlet.
 The reason it is not the overall pick is capacity: 2.1 fridge days against
4.1, and it does not expand, so the capacity you buy is the capacity you own
 forever.
Both entry units share the one limitation nobody mentions in the listings: the 12V car input.
 Most vehicle sockets are fused at 10 to 15A, which caps charging near 120 to 180 watts, so
 refilling a 1kWh station from the cigarette lighter takes the better part of a driving day. If
 you plan to lean on driving to charge, budget for a wired 12V input at 8A or better and treat
 the socket as a trickle rather than a charging strategy.
 How do you recharge one in a vehicle without waiting all day?
There are three inputs and they are not equal. Wall power is fastest and irrelevant off-grid.
 Solar is the one that makes a station a real off-grid system. The 12V vehicle socket is the one
 everybody tries first and the one that disappoints.
For solar, the useful arithmetic is: daily watt-hours equals panel watts multiplied by peak sun
 hours multiplied by a system derate of 0.75 for a flat
 roof-mounted array through an MPPT controller. A 200W panel at 5 peak sun hours therefore
 returns roughly 750Wh , which is about 59 amp-hours at 12.8V.
 That is one fridge day plus a little, from one panel, on a good day. Two panels turn a station
 into something that does not go backwards.
A portable panel you aim at the sun outproduces the same wattage lying flat on a roof by a wide
 margin, and it is the only option if you camp in trees. The
 EcoFlow 220W bifacial portable panel at
under $500 plugs into an EcoFlow station without an adapter hunt, which sounds trivial and is the
 single most common source of a returned solar order. A fixed roof array trades that peak output
 for never having to set anything out, which is the right trade if you move camp daily.
 How much of the pack does a fridge really take?
More than the sticker suggests and less than people fear. A compressor fridge does not draw
 continuously, it cycles. The published draw is what the compressor takes while running, and the
 number that empties a battery is that figure multiplied by duty cycle, which is driven almost
 entirely by ambient temperature and insulation quality.
In practical terms, a well insulated 45 litre unit like the
 ICECO VL45 at under $1,000 sits nearer 30 amp-hours a
 day in mild weather and climbs toward 45 in desert heat with the vehicle closed up. A thinner
 walled budget box of the same volume can be half again as thirsty in the same conditions, which
 is why insulation quality is a battery sizing decision rather than a comfort one. The
 12V fridge roundup explains which units earn the premium
 and which ones quietly cost you a second battery.
Two habits cut the number materially. Park the fridge out of direct sun and give it air on all
 sides, because a compressor venting into a sealed cabinet works against itself. And pre-cool the
 contents before the trip, since pulling warm groceries down to temperature on day one is often
 the single biggest draw of the whole weekend.
 When does a station stop making sense and a DIY bank start?
The crossover is not about capacity, it is about charging. A station charges from a vehicle at
 roughly 100 to 400 watts depending on the input it offers. A wired DC-DC charger feeding a
 lithium house battery charges at 600 watts and up, which turns a two hour drive into a full
 refill. Once your travel pattern involves daily driving and daily heavy use, the wired system
 wins by a distance that no amount of extra station capacity closes.
Cost per usable amp-hour also flips. Two kilowatt-hours of station sits near under $1,000, while a
 200Ah lithium bank plus a charger and an inverter delivers more usable energy for a similar
 total and can be repaired component by component. What you pay for in the DIY version is your
 own labour, a real fusing plan and the risk that comes with both. The
 power station versus DIY battery bank 
comparison walks the whole decision end to end.
 Who should not buy the expert tier?
Do not buy the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 at
under $5,000 unless you have already measured a daily load that a 2kWh unit cannot cover. It
 weighs 113.5 lb, which makes it a payload decision before it is a power decision:
 that is most of the remaining margin on a loaded mid-size SUV once you have added a rooftop
 tent, water and recovery gear. Run the numbers through the
 payload weight calculator before you order,
 not after.
Do not agonise between the EcoFlow Delta 3 Max at
under $1,000 and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at
under $1,000, because they are the same 2kWh class within about one percent of capacity and
 within a few cents per watt-hour of each other. The Max adds faster AC recharging, about
1 hour from a wall outlet by the maker's figure, and that is exactly the
 thing you will not have on the trips this site is about. The Elite adds
200W more inverter and weighs
1.5 lb less. Buy the Max if you already own
 EcoFlow panels or routinely turn around at home mid-week. Otherwise the Elite is the pick.
And do not buy any 2kWh unit as a first purchase if your camping is currently one or two nights
 at a time. A under $500 station that gets used every weekend is a better outcome than a
under $1,000 station that stays in the garage because it is too heavy to bother lifting.
 Capacity you never discharge is money parked, and lithium ages on the shelf as well as in use.
 What do people get wrong when they buy one?
 Reading peak inverter watts as continuous watts. A 1800W station will surge higher for a second or two, and that surge figure is not a licence to run a 1800W kettle for ten minutes.
 Ignoring the solar input ceiling. Buying 600W of panels for a station that accepts 200W wastes two thirds of the array and all of the money.
 Charging from the cigarette socket and calling solar a failure. The socket is the bottleneck, not the panels.
 Forgetting the standby draw. Leaving the AC inverter switched on with nothing plugged in quietly costs 10 to 20 watts continuously, which is 240 to 480 watt-hours a day, or roughly half a small station.
 Storing it fully charged in a hot vehicle. Lithium keeps best around half charge in a cool place, and the difference over several years is real.
 Skipping the weight check. Everything in the expert tier is 50 lb or more, and roof and payload limits are unforgiving.
If this is your first electrical purchase for a vehicle, start at the
 overland power for beginners guide , which
 lays out the whole decision in order: load first, storage second, charging third, and hardware
 last. The station is the answer to two of those four questions at once, which is exactly why it
 is such a good first purchase and such a poor last one.
Want a smaller unit for a fridge-only setup? See the specs for the
 Dometic PLB15 and the
 Dometic PLB40 , and the
 van electrical system guide for how a station fits into a full build.
 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best portable power station for a vehicle build? For most vehicle builds the pick in this guide is the Bluetti Elite 200 V2: 2,073Wh of LiFePO4 capacity and a 2,600W inverter, roughly 162 amp-hours at 12.8V, enough to run a 45 quart fridge for about four days with no charging. Smaller and larger units are compared in the tiers above, ranked by watt-hours, inverter output and recharge speed. This is a researched comparison, not a lab review.
 What size portable power station do I need for a 12V fridge? A 45 quart compressor fridge draws roughly 30 to 45 amp-hours a day at 90F ambient, which is about 400 to 550 watt-hours. A 1kWh station such as the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at under $500 therefore runs a fridge for about 2.1 days with nothing else plugged in, and about a day and a half once you add lights and phone charging. A 2kWh station such as the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at under $1,000 roughly doubles that to 4.1 days. Anything under 500Wh is a one-night unit.
 Can a portable power station replace a proper house battery? For weekend use, yes. A station is a battery, an inverter, a charge controller and a fuse block in one case, already assembled and already certified. What it cannot do is charge at high current from the alternator, hide under a bed, or scale past its own expansion limit. Full-time builds usually outgrow one, which is why the expandable models hold their value better than the sealed ones.
 How long does it take to recharge a power station while driving? From a 12V cigarette socket, very slowly. Most sockets are fused at 10 to 15A, which caps you near 120 to 180 watts, so a 1kWh station needs six to eight hours of driving. A dedicated wired 12V input at 8A or better, or a DC-DC charger feeding an Anderson connector, moves that to roughly two or three hours. Solar at 200W adds around 750 watt-hours on a clear day.
 Is LiFePO4 worth paying more for in a power station? Yes, and every station on this page uses it. LiFePO4 tolerates the shallow partial cycling a vehicle build inflicts on a battery every single day, and rated cycle life is typically 3,000 to 4,000 cycles against 500 or so for the older NMC packs. It is also far more tolerant of heat, which matters when the station lives in a closed vehicle parked in the sun.
 Can I use a power station below freezing? You can discharge one below freezing, but LiFePO4 cannot safely accept charge below 32F without internal heating. Most stations refuse to charge when the pack is cold and simply show an error, which reads like a fault and is actually the battery management system doing its job. Bring the unit inside the cab or the tent overnight and it will charge normally once the cells are above freezing.
 Do I need a 2000Wh station or will 1000Wh do? One kilowatt-hour covers a fridge, lights, a laptop and phone charging for two days, and it recharges from a 200W array in about a day and a half of good sun. Two kilowatt-hours is the point where you can stop rationing and run a coffee grinder or an induction burner briefly. Buy 1kWh if you drive most days and 2kWh if you sit still for three or four.
 How we choose: we compare published
 manufacturer specifications, standards documents including ABYC E-11, and verified owner
 reviews. We do not test gear in person. Vehicle payload, roof load and charging limits vary by
 model and year, so confirm yours against the door jamb sticker and the owner's manual rather
 than any number published here.

Best Portable Power Station for RV Boondocking | WattPicks 
 Skip to content 
 Best RV Power Stations for Boondocking and Shore Power
 RV power is a different job than camping or home backup: you need a shore-power plug, honest usable watt-hours, and enough continuous AC to start what you actually own. Here are four stations that fit real RV loads — and the ones to skip.
 Avery Nolan — WattPicks founding editor. Avery sizes stations for camping, RV and outages from published Wh, watts and cost-per-Wh — no invented lab scores.
 Share 
 Affiliate disclosure We may earn a commission from qualifying purchases at no extra cost to you.
 What an RV actually asks of a power station
 The question I get most is some version of: can I run my camper off one of these instead of firing up a generator? The honest answer depends less on the headline watt-hour number than on three things — whether the unit has a shore-power outlet you can plug a 30A RV cord into, how much of that capacity you can actually pull out, and whether the continuous AC rating clears the appliances you plan to start.
 This page is for boondocking and shore-power-style RV use: a fridge, a CPAP, fans, lights, a laptop, maybe a coffee maker or a short burst of air conditioning. It is not a whole-home backup guide, and it is not a generator replacement for a 50A coach running two air conditioners all afternoon. If that is your job, you want a different class of equipment entirely.
 Four hard requirements shaped this shortlist. A real AC outlet count you can live with. A continuous rating that matches camper loads rather than surge marketing. LiFePO4 chemistry, because you will cycle this thing constantly and lead-acid or NMC packs age faster under that treatment. And a recharge path that works off shore power, solar, or the tow vehicle — ideally all three.
 One disclosure up front: this page uses Amazon Associates links, and I may earn a commission if you buy through them. The picks are fit-led. Where a cheaper unit wins on a given job, it wins here too.
 Quick picks
 Top pick for RV shore power: the BLUETTI Elite 300. It is the only unit here with a TT-30 outlet and a 12V/30A DC output, which means you can plug the coach in directly instead of chaining adapters. The 3,014 Wh pack and 2,400W continuous output cover a fridge, fans, and a short AC run.
 Runner-up and the value pick: the BLUETTI AC180. At $499 it is the cheapest per nameplate watt-hour of the four at $0.43/Wh, it has four AC outlets, and owners report a genuinely seamless UPS handoff. It is the right answer for a smaller camper or a van build where you are not trying to run air conditioning.
 Also consider: the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 if portability is the priority — 23.8 lb is carryable in a way the others are not — and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max if you want the fastest recharge and the best UPS behavior and can live without a TT-30.
 Budget note: none of these include a solar panel, and only the Elite 300 has a native TT-30. If you plan to recharge off solar or plug in a 30A cord, add the cost of a compatible panel and a quality adapter to the station price before you compare.

 How I weighted this job
 I scored each station on four weighted factors. Usable capacity and RV load fit got 35% — that means nameplate Wh adjusted for the reality that inverters burn idle power and most units reserve a slice of the pack. Continuous AC output and outlet layout got 25%, because a TT-30 or a true 20A blade outlet changes what you can plug in without an adapter. Recharge speed and solar flexibility got 25%, since boondocking lives or dies on how fast you refill. Build, weight, and owner-reported reliability took the last 15%.
 The evidence behind those scores is listing specs plus the owner themes on file for each unit — the things people actually complain about after a season, like idle draw, flaky wireless pads, and solar voltage windows that reject their panels. Those are home-user checks against published specs, not lab-bench measurements, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
 Why the BLUETTI Elite 300 edges out the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max at the top: both are 2400W units, but the Elite 300 carries a TT-30 RV outlet and a 12V/30A DC output that the DELTA 3 Max does not list, and that is the single biggest practical difference for a camper. The DELTA 3 Max wins on recharge speed and app polish, and it is the better UPS. On the RV-specific weights, the outlet layout decides it.
 Scoreboard on those weights:
 • BLUETTI Elite 300 — High on RV outlet fit and capacity; Med on continuous watts. List $1699.
 • EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max — High on recharge speed and UPS behavior; Med on RV outlet fit (no TT-30). List $1199.
 • BLUETTI AC180 — High on value and outlet count; Med on usable capacity for small loads. List $499.
 • Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 — High on portability; Med on capacity and solar input. List $559.
 That is why the pick splits by job rather than one universal winner.
 Scenario facts: what camper loads actually draw
 These are typical draw bands, not measurements of your specific appliance. Check the label on your own gear before you buy — a 12V compressor fridge and a residential fridge are not the same load.
 Solar panels are sold separately on every unit here — none of these picks include a panel.
 A 30A RV shore-power cord needs a TT-30 outlet or a proper adapter; check before you assume.
 Inverter idle draw (often 15–20W) quietly eats capacity on small overnight loads.

 Spec snapshot
 Prices are current list prices, not sale stickers. Ratings are the listing aggregate, which is a popularity signal, not proof of long-term durability.
