 The ranking
 Ranked on the weights above. Nameplate $/Wh is shown for reference; the cheapest per nameplate watt-hour is the AC180 at $0.43/Wh, and I am not going to crown anything else on cost.
 #1 BLUETTI Elite 300 — $1699, 3014 Wh, 2400 W, 58 lb, $0.56/Wh
 #2 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max — $1199, 2048 Wh, 2400 W, 44.8 lb, $0.59/Wh
 #3 BLUETTI AC180 — $499, 1152 Wh, 1800 W, 35.3 lb, $0.43/Wh
 #4 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 — $559, 1070 Wh, 1500 W, 23.8 lb, $0.52/Wh
 #1 BLUETTI Elite 300: the one that plugs into the coach
 The Elite 300 earns the top spot on outlet layout, not on capacity alone. It has a TT-30 RV outlet and a 12V/30A DC output, which means a camper can plug the shore-power cord straight in and run 12V loads like a fridge, water pump, or diesel heater without a pile of adapters. That is a specific RV feature the other three do not list, and it is worth real money if you are actually boondocking in a coach.
 In use, the density is the story: a 3,014 Wh pack in a body narrower than older 2 kWh stations, with handles that grip and a big color display readable from across the site. One owner reported pushing a continuous ~2400W multi-appliance load for about half an hour and it held without complaint, and the UPS handoff kept a connected computer alive through a power transition with no dropout. On a DC-only overnight run it barely sipped — one owner finished four nights on a CPAP with over a week of charge left.
 The caveats are real and you should hear them before you spend $1699. There is no battery expansion, so you are locked to the built-in capacity. The solar input window is tight — roughly 12–60V at ~20–22A — which means many rigid panels cannot reach the 1,200W ceiling, and pushing open-circuit voltage past the limit can damage the MPPT and void the warranty per the manual. Check your panel specs before you buy, not after. Some settings live only in the app, firmware updates are Wi-Fi only, and the soft-start ramp means high-inrush inductive loads can balk — one owner could not start a 500W dehumidifier on first switch-on. Fan hum is present under load, and at 58 lb it is a two-hand lift.
 Suits: RV owners who want to plug the coach in directly and run a fridge, fans, and a short AC session. Skip if: you need expandable capacity, plan to run big inductive appliances routinely, or already own rigid panels outside that voltage window.
 #2 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max: fastest refill, best UPS
 The DELTA 3 Max is the unit I would hand someone who cares most about recharge speed and clean switchover. It refills to 100% in a little over an hour, and the 10ms transfer made it a credible UPS substitute — during a real outage one owner arrived at 29% and still carried a laptop, a modem, and three pedestal fans for hours before topping off. On a fridge test, one owner reported an iceco VL45Pro at 36°F ran a little over five days.
 At 2,048 Wh and 2,400W continuous it sits between the Elite 300 and the AC180 on capacity, and it is lighter than the Elite 300 at 44.8 lb. Four AC outlets, and the app's storm guard is genuinely useful for remote status checks. The 2,400W continuous rating covers a microwave or a coffee maker without drama.
 Two things keep it at #2. First, no TT-30 or 12V/30A output is listed, so an RV shore-power cord needs an adapter — that is the practical gap versus the Elite 300. Second, USB-C tops out at 100W, and one owner with a large EcoFlow collection specifically wanted a 140W port. The review base is also thinner than the others here, and most high-helpful notes are short on long-term durability, so I would treat it as promising rather than proven over years.
 Suits: home-backup and RV users who want the fastest recharge and the best UPS behavior, and who can live with an adapter for shore power. Skip if: a native TT-30 outlet matters to you, you need a 140W USB-C output, or you want a long track record before buying.
 #3 BLUETTI AC180: the value pick for smaller campers
 The AC180 is the cheapest per nameplate watt-hour here at $0.43/Wh, and for a van or a small travel trailer it is often the right size. Four AC outlets, 1,800W continuous, and a UPS handoff that owners describe as seamless — one wired it into a basement circuit and the internet and devices never blinked when grid power dropped. Recharge is quick: over 1,000W from the wall after a full discharge, roughly two hours at standard speed.
 The honest part is usable capacity. With the inverter on, the unit pulls roughly 15–20W idle, and the manual reserves about 10% of the pack, so real usable energy is well under the 1,152 Wh nameplate — small overnight loads feel that most. The wireless charging pad on top is flaky; it connects then quits after seconds, and that complaint repeats across owners. Some settings, including charge rate, live only in the app, and a couple of owners needed firmware updates before the unit performed to spec. At 35.3 lb it is fine to move spot to spot, not to carry far.
 Suits: smaller campers and van builds where 1,800W continuous covers the loads and you want the lowest cost per nameplate watt-hour. Skip if: you need every rated watt-hour for tiny loads, you expect the wireless pad to work, or you are trying to run air conditioning.
 #4 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2: the carryable one
 At 23.8 lb the Explorer 1000 v2 is the only unit here you can reasonably carry from the truck to the picnic table, and that portability is its whole case. One owner set it up with a fridge and a portable AC running at the same time, and quiet mode dropped the noise enough that they slept while it powered the fridge and a few fans. Recharge from empty ran about 1h40m on normal mode; the emergency boost goes higher but snaps back after each quick charge. A 12-quart DC fridge in eco mode went three days from 100% to 43% with three phone top-ups mixed in.
 The trade-offs are clear at 1,070 Wh and 1,500W continuous. There are no 12V barrel ports, so 12V gear needs an adapter off the cigarette socket. Solar tops out around 400W and is slow, with panel angle needing constant nudging. It will not carry big loads — a 1700W air fryer is out, and a 12" sliding miter saw spun a quarter turn and quit. The buttons sit deep in the case, and Wi-Fi does not hold overnight, so checking status means reconnecting.
 Suits: weekend campers and small-trailer owners who prioritize lifting and carrying over capacity, and who run a fridge, fans, and electronics rather than appliances. Skip if: you need native 12V ports, serious solar input, or high-watt appliance runs.
 What goes wrong on RV power setups
 These are the mistakes I see repeated in owner notes, and they cost real money.
 Buying on nameplate Wh and ignoring idle draw. A 1,152 Wh unit with a 15–20W inverter load and a 10% reserve delivers noticeably less than the label suggests on small overnight loads.
 Mismatching solar panels to the input window. The Elite 300's tight voltage range rejects many rigid panels, and exceeding open-circuit voltage can damage the MPPT and void the warranty per the manual. Match panels to the spec sheet first.
 Assuming a shore-power cord plugs in directly. Only the Elite 300 lists a TT-30 outlet; the others need an adapter, and cheap adapters heat up.
 Expecting air conditioning to run for hours. A 13,500 BTU RV AC draws 1,200–1,600W running with a higher startup, so even a 3,014 Wh pack gives you a couple of hours, not an afternoon.
 Forgetting that solar panels are sold separately on every unit here. Budget for the panel and the cable, not just the station.
 Who should pick something else
 If you are running a 50A coach with two air conditioners and a residential fridge, none of these four is the right tool. You want a properly installed inverter/charger system with a large lithium bank, or a generator — a portable station is a supplement, not a replacement at that scale.
 If your only job is keeping a CPAP and a phone alive overnight, you are overbuying here. A much smaller, lighter station will do it for a fraction of the price, and the 58 lb Elite 300 is a poor fit for a tent.
 And if you need expandable capacity over years, the Elite 300 is the wrong pick specifically because it has no battery expansion — the AC180 and DELTA 3 Max are better starting points if you expect your needs to grow, though neither lists a native TT-30 either.
 What owners keep saying
 Themes from the review packs on file, paraphrased. Listing aggregates are shown for context only — they are not proof of long-term durability.
 Elite 300 (4.7 listing aggregate): owners praise the compact size for a 3 kWh pack and the RV shore-power plug, and repeatedly flag the tight solar voltage window and lack of expansion.
 Explorer 1000 v2 (4.7): fridge-overnight and quiet-mode stories dominate; the recurring complaints are the missing 12V barrel ports and the ceiling on high-watt appliances.
 AC180 (4.5): the UPS handoff and fast recharge get the most praise; idle draw and the flaky wireless pad are the most repeated gripes.
 DELTA 3 Max (4.7): the 10ms transfer and roughly one-hour recharge come up constantly; the review base is thinner, so long-term durability is not yet well established.
 Frequently asked
 Can the Elite 300 run my RV air conditioner?
 It lists 2,400W continuous with a 4,800W surge, and one owner reported running a 15,000 BTU Coleman RV AC for about two hours. Expect hours, not an afternoon, and check your AC's running and startup draw.
 Do any of these include solar panels?
 No. Panels are sold separately on all four, and the Explorer 1000 v2 is compatible only with Jackery panels for solar charging.
 Which is cheapest per watt-hour?
 On nameplate $/Wh, the BLUETTI AC180 at $0.43/Wh. That is nameplate, not usable — idle draw and reserve cut into real output on every unit here.
 Can I plug my 30A RV cord straight into the DELTA 3 Max or AC180?
 Neither lists a TT-30 outlet, so you need an adapter. The Elite 300 is the one with a native TT-30.

Quick answer: For most RVers, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 is the best portable power station for RV use — 2048Wh of LFP capacity, a 2400W inverter, and 800W solar input cover a weekend or a week off-grid. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is the runner-up: nearly identical capacity for $300 less, with a slightly smaller surge ceiling.
 Why RVs Need a Different Power Station Than Camping or Home Backup
 An RV is not a tent and it is not a house. It already has a converter, a house battery, and often shore power and generator hookups, so a portable power station is not your only power source — it is a supplement that fills specific gaps: quiet overnight power without running the generator, backup when the house battery is depleted, or a dedicated circuit for a CPAP, laptop, or mini-fridge that you do not want tied to the rig's main electrical system. That changes the buying calculus. You need enough continuous wattage to run real RV loads (a residential fridge draws 100-200W continuous with 1000W+ startup surge, a window AC draws 900-1500W), enough capacity to bridge a night or two without shore power, fast solar or AC recharging so you are not waiting all day, and a form factor that survives vibration, dust, and temperature swings on the road.
 Best Portable Power Stations for RV: Comparison Table
 Power Station Capacity Continuous Output Weight Price Best For 
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 2048Wh (LFP) 2400W (4000W surge) 49.4 lb $1,299 Full-time RVers, boondocking 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 2042Wh (LFP) 2200W (4400W surge) 43.5 lb $999 Best value, weekender to full-timer 
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 1024Wh (LFP) 2000W (3000W surge) 27.6 lb $699 Weekend trips, mid-size trailers 
 Anker SOLIX C300 288Wh (LFP) 300W AC charge, 140W USB-C PD ~7.7 lb $249 Truck campers, backup for phones/CPAP/laptops 
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2: Best Overall for RV Life
 The C2000 Gen 2 is built for people who live in their rig for stretches at a time, not just weekend trips. Its 2048Wh LFP pack and 2400W continuous inverter (4000W surge) run a residential fridge, a microwave, a coffee maker, and a laptop without load-shedding, and the 800W solar input means a couple of 200W panels on the roof or laid out at camp can realistically replace what you use in a sunny day. At 49.4 lb it is not something you carry far, but it is designed to live bolted or strapped into a cabinet, not backpacked. The standout for RV use specifically is the 1200W AC charge input and quiet 25dB operation — you can top it off from a campground pedestal in about an hour without it sounding like a box fan next to your bed.
 Trade-offs: at $1,299 it is the most expensive station on this list, and nearly 50 lb is a lot to move if you need to relocate it between the rig and a campsite.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 price on Amazon 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2: Best Value for the Capacity
 The Explorer 2000 v2 gets you into the same 2kWh capacity tier as the C2000 Gen 2 for $300 less. Jackery's brand recognition and wide accessory ecosystem (solar panels, transfer switches, expansion batteries) make it an easy default if this is your first large power station and you want parts to be easy to find later. The 4400W surge ceiling is actually higher than the Anker's, which matters if you are running something with a hard motor-start spike, like a rooftop AC compressor or a residential fridge compressor kicking on.
 Trade-offs: at 43.5 lb it is only marginally lighter than the C2000 Gen 2, the AC recharge is slower (1100W vs 1200W input, and a less refined charge curve), and it lacks the C2000's ultra-quiet fan profile.
 Check the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 price on Amazon 
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: Best for Weekend Trips and Mid-Size Trailers
 Not everyone needs 2kWh. If your RV use is weekends and week-long trips rather than full-time boondocking, the C1000 Gen 2's 1024Wh capacity and 2000W inverter cover the essentials — lighting, device charging, a CPAP overnight, a coffee maker in the morning — without the size, weight, or price of the 2kWh-class units. Its class-leading 49-minute AC recharge means you can top it off during a lunch stop at a campground with shore power and be back to full before you leave.
 Trade-offs: 1024Wh will not carry a residential fridge or a window AC for long, and it has no solar input spec published at the same level as the larger C2000 Gen 2, so treat it as an AC-recharge-first unit.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 price on Amazon 
 Anker SOLIX C300: Best Compact Backup for Truck Campers
 For truck campers, teardrops, and anyone who just wants a dedicated power source for phones, a laptop, and a CPAP rather than running the whole rig, the C300's 288Wh pack is enough for 4-5 laptop charges or 4-6 hours of CPAP use. Its 140W USB-C PD port is the fastest laptop charging of any station on this list relative to its size, and at under 8 lb it is the only one you would comfortably hand-carry to a picnic table.
 Trade-offs: 288Wh will not touch fridge or AC loads, and there is no meaningful continuous AC wattage for larger appliances — this is a device-charging and small-load unit, not a house-power replacement.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C300 price on Amazon 
 How Much Power Station Capacity Does an RV Actually Need?
 Start with what you are trying to power and for how long, not the biggest number you can afford. A 12V compressor fridge draws roughly 40-60Wh per hour of runtime (it cycles, so real draw is lower than its rated wattage), which is about 1000-1400Wh over 24 hours — within reach of a single 2kWh station if it is your only load. A residential-style AC fridge draws more, closer to 1500-2500Wh per day. A window or mini-split AC unit is the real capacity killer: even a small 5,000 BTU unit can pull 400-600W continuous, which will drain a 2kWh station in under four hours of straight running, so AC use should be treated as a generator or shore-power task, not a power-station task, unless you are running one of the very large stations built for it. For most RVers, sizing to cover lighting, device charging, a fridge, and occasional small appliances for 1-2 days without recharge — call it 1,500-2,500Wh of usable capacity — hits the sweet spot. Use our power station wattage calculator to size your specific load list before buying.
 Solar Charging on the Road
 Solar is what makes a power station genuinely useful for extended RV travel instead of just glorified shore-power storage. The C2000 Gen 2 and Explorer 2000 v2 both accept up to 800W of solar input, which under good sun can recharge a depleted 2kWh unit in 2-3 hours — fast enough to fully reset overnight usage before you break camp. Portable panels are easier for RVers than roof-mounted ones because you can angle them toward the sun and move them into shade-free spots at each new site, rather than being stuck with whatever angle your roof happens to face. See our guide on choosing solar panels for a power station for panel wattage and connector compatibility.
 RV-Specific Connections: Shore Power, 30A, and Transfer Switches
 If you want a power station to feed part of your RV's existing wiring rather than just running loose extension cords to individual appliances, you need to think about how it connects. Most portable power stations output standard NEMA 5-15 household outlets, not the 30A or 50A shore-power plugs RVs use, so you will need an adapter or a properly installed transfer switch to route power into your rig's breaker panel safely — never back-feed a panel without a transfer switch. Our guide on connecting a power station to an RV 30A outlet covers the adapter path, and understanding NEMA TT-30 and RV adapter compatibility explains which adapter matches which rig. For a broader look at built-in RV integration features across brands, see our roundup of power stations with the best RV and camper integration .
 Common Mistakes RVers Make When Choosing a Power Station
 The most common error is buying based on capacity alone and ignoring continuous wattage — a 2kWh station with only a 1000W inverter cannot run a microwave or a hair dryer even though it has plenty of stored energy. The second is skipping solar input specs entirely: a station that only recharges from AC shore power is far less useful once you are boondocking for more than a night. The third is buying a unit too heavy to move between the rig and a campsite when you actually wanted portability, or conversely buying a lightweight small-capacity unit and expecting it to run a fridge for days. Match the unit to your actual trip style — weekend camper, full-time boondocker, or backup-only — rather than the biggest sale price you see.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a portable power station run my RV air conditioner? Only briefly, and only the largest stations. A small 5,000 BTU unit needs 400-600W continuous with a startup surge that can spike past 1500W, which will drain even a 2kWh station in a few hours. For sustained AC use, plan on shore power or a generator, and treat a power station as backup for everything else.
 What size power station do I need for a weekend RV trip? For lighting, device charging, and a CPAP or small fridge over a weekend without recharging, 1,000-1,500Wh of capacity with at least a 1500W inverter is usually enough. Use our wattage calculator to total your specific appliance list before deciding.
 Is it safe to wire a power station into my RVs electrical panel? Only with a properly installed transfer switch that prevents the power station and shore power or generator from being connected simultaneously. Running loose extension cords to individual appliances is simpler and safer for most RVers than panel integration.
 How long does it take to recharge a power station with RV solar? A 2kWh-class station with 800W of solar input can recharge from empty in roughly 2-3 hours under strong, direct sun, though cloud cover, panel angle, and shading from trees at a campsite will meaningfully slow that down.
 Should I buy one large power station or two smaller ones for an RV? One large station is simpler to manage and charges faster overall, but two smaller units let you run one at the rig while carrying the other to a picnic table or tent site, and give you redundancy if one fails mid-trip. Full-time RVers often prefer one large unit; occasional campers benefit more from a mid-size unit plus a compact backup like the SOLIX C300.
